title: Iran vows 'every means' against US blockade as Treasury targets its shadow banks
dek: Tehran answered President Trump's threat to sink tankers that run the blockade. Washington sanctioned 30 targets in Iran's payment network, and the Houthis claimed a strike on a Saudi refinery.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran said on Monday it would use "every means" to counter the United States' naval blockade of its ports, a day after President Donald Trump warned that Iranian ships trying to break it would be sent "to the bottom of the sea". Hours later the US Treasury imposed sanctions on 22 companies and eight people it said formed part of Iran's "shadow banking" network for oil payments.

"We will certainly not tolerate this situation and will use every means to counter US aggression," the foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, told his weekly press briefing in Tehran, calling the blockade a violation of the UN Charter and "an act of crime", according to reports. Asked on Sunday about calls in Iran for a convoy of tankers to break the blockade, Mr Trump said: "I hope they do it; they'll all go down to the bottom of the sea, just like the rest of their navy."

## What Washington did

The Treasury said its action, the latest under what it calls Operation Economic Outcast, targeted exchange houses in Iran and front companies, most of them in Dubai and others in Hong Kong and Turkey, that it said process payments for Iranian oil, petrochemical and metals exporters. Among them is the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which matches exporters earning foreign currency with importers, and a Dubai firm the Treasury said handled payments for the National Iranian Tanker Company. "Iran's shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the release.

In a separate notice, the Treasury's financial crimes unit, FinCEN, said it had identified about $14.7 billion of financial activity between January 2025 and August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking, with recipients in the United Arab Emirates receiving about 52 per cent. It said suspicious-activity reports are leads, not proof of wrongdoing. No India-based person or company was named in Monday's designations.

## The view from Tehran

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within hours once the other side meets its commitments. Mr Baghaei listed Iran's conditions as lifting US sanctions, ending the blockade and carrying out what Washington accepted under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, reports said. Mr Trump has declared that memorandum void. Qatar's prime minister was due to meet Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday as part of Doha's mediation; no outcome had been reported by Tuesday morning.

## Claims at sea and on land

Iran's navy said several tankers had caught fire in the strait after striking mines; no maritime authority had confirmed this, and the claims could not be verified. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said on Sunday that military forces were involved in an incident with an oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, without saying whose. US Central Command had not commented.

In Yemen, the Houthi movement said it had scored "a direct hit" on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh refinery on the Red Sea coast, home to the Petro Rabigh complex run with Japan's Sumitomo Chemical. The Saudi-led coalition's spokesman, Turki al-Malki, said air defences had "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" fired towards the western region. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed any damage. The Red Sea coast matters more than usual now: Saudi Arabia has been moving crude by pipeline to its western ports to avoid Hormuz.

## Why it matters for India

India imports most of its crude oil and much of its gas, and a large share normally passes through Hormuz. An attack on the LPG tanker MT Tara Gas on 16 November left one Indian sailor missing. Monday's sanctions also matter for Indian shipping and trading firms that deal with Gulf traders, because doing business with a designated company can expose them to US penalties. Brent crude was trading near $89 a barrel late on Monday, down about 3 per cent on the day, according to market data. New Delhi had made no statement on the latest exchanges by Tuesday morning.
